segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There was a man in Caesarea named Cornelius, a centurion of what was called the Italian Cohort,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: a devout man who feared God along with his whole household; he did many acts of charity for the people and prayed to God continually.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God coming in to him and saying to him,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Cornelius!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He stared at him, terrified, and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What is it, lord?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The angel said to him,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Your prayers and your acts of charity have gone up as a memorial before God.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: Now send men to Joppa and send for a certain Simon, who is called Peter.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: He is lodging with a certain Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the angel who spoke to him had gone, he called two of his household slaves and a devout soldier from among those who attended him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and after explaining everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The next day, as they were on their way and approaching the city, Peter went up on the roof to pray, about the sixth hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He became hungry and wanted to eat. But while they were preparing a meal, a trance came over him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he saw heaven opened and an object coming down, something like a large sheet, being lowered to the earth by its four corners.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In it were all the four-footed animals and crawling creatures of the earth and birds of the sky.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And a voice came to him:

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “Get up, Peter; slaughter and eat.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Peter said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Certainly not, Lord, for I have never eaten anything defiled or unclean.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The voice came to him again, a second time:

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “What God has made clean, you must not call defiled.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This happened three times, and at once the object was taken up into heaven.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now while Peter was at a loss within himself about what the vision he had seen might mean, just then the men sent by Cornelius, having asked their way to Simon’s house, arrived at the gate.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They called out and asked whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While Peter was still thinking over the vision, the Spirit said to him,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “There are men here looking for you.

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: Get up, go down, and go with them without hesitating at all, for I have sent them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter went down to the men and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Here I am, the one you are looking for. What is the reason you have come?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Cornelius, a centurion, a righteous man who fears God and is well spoken of by the whole nation of the Jews, was instructed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he invited them in and gave them lodging. The next day he got up and set out with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa went along with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the following day he entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As Peter was about to go in, Cornelius met him, fell at his feet, and paid him homage.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Peter raised him up, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Stand up; I too am a human being.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Talking with him, he went in and found many people gathered.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You yourselves know how forbidden it is for a Jewish man to associate with or visit someone of another people. But God has shown me that I should call no person defiled or unclean.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: That is why I came without objection when I was sent for. So I ask, for what reason did you send for me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Cornelius said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Four days ago, at this very hour, I was in my house praying at the ninth hour, and suddenly a man in shining clothing stood before me

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard, and your acts of charity have been remembered before God.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So send to Joppa and summon Simon, who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So I sent to you at once, and you were kind enough to come. Now then, we are all here in the presence of God to hear everything the Lord has commanded you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Peter opened his mouth and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “In truth, I am grasping that God shows no partiality,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: but in every nation the one who fears him and practices righteousness is acceptable to him.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: You know the word that he sent to the children of Israel, announcing the good news of peace through Jesus Christ—he is Lord of all.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: You yourselves know what took place throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, and how he went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: We are witnesses of everything he did, both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. And they put him to death by hanging him on a tree.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: God raised him on the third day and granted that he be plainly seen,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: not by all the people but by witnesses whom God had chosen beforehand—by us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: He commanded us to proclaim to the people and to testify solemnly that he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: To him all the prophets bear witness, that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell on all who were listening to the word.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The believers from among the circumcised, all who had come with Peter, were astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out on the Gentiles too,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for they heard them speaking in tongues and praising the greatness of God. Then Peter responded,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Can anyone withhold the water and keep these people from being baptized, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we did?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he ordered that they be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay on for some days.

notes.note: A cohort was a Roman army unit of several hundred soldiers, and a centurion commanded a subdivision of roughly eighty to a hundred men. Caesarea was the seat of the Roman administration of Judea. A cohort with this name is attested in the region by inscriptions, though whether it was stationed at Caesarea at this date is debated.

Luke uses this expression for Gentiles who worshiped Israel’s God and were attached to the synagogue without becoming full converts, which for men meant circumcision. “The people” in the same verse is Luke’s regular term for Israel, so the charity was given to Jews. Scholars debate how formal a category “God-fearers” was.

The Greek word means charitable giving to the poor, which Jewish piety ranked alongside prayer. “Alms” is accurate but has largely dropped out of ordinary English; many modern translations paraphrase with “gave generously to those in need”. The same rendering is used in verses 4 and 31.

Hours were counted from sunrise, so the ninth hour is about three in the afternoon. It was the time of the afternoon sacrifice and prayer in the Jerusalem temple, which suggests that Cornelius kept Jewish hours of prayer. The sixth hour in verse 9 is about noon.

In the Greek Old Testament this word names the portion of an offering burned on the altar so that it rises to God (as in Leviticus 2). The angel describes a Gentile’s prayers and charity in the language of temple sacrifice: they have “gone up” and been accepted.

The word’s everyday sense is “shared, common”, but in Jewish usage it meant ritually profane, unfit for a people set apart to God. “Common” (KJV, ESV) now suggests merely “ordinary”; other versions have “profane” or “impure”. “Defiled” follows the traditional rendering of the same word in Mark 7. The related verb in verse 15 and the adjective in verse 28 are rendered to match.

The verb can mean “to hesitate, to doubt” or “to make a distinction, to discriminate”. Most translations take it as hesitation here. The other sense, “making no distinction” between Jew and Gentile, is also possible and is probably in view when Peter retells the event in the next chapter.

One Greek word lies behind “nation” here and in verse 35 and “Gentiles” in verse 45. In the singular it means a people or nation, including the Jewish nation; in the plural it commonly means the non-Jewish peoples. English has to choose by context.

The verb means to prostrate oneself in reverence, and what the gesture signifies depends on who receives it. Most translations have “worshiped” here, and Peter’s reply shows he considered the reverence excessive for a mere human. Since Cornelius, a worshiper of Israel’s God, is unlikely to have taken Peter for a deity, “paid him homage” is used; some scholars think Luke does intend an improper act of worship.

The word describes what offends against established custom or sacred order, something taboo, and is not the usual term for breaking a written law. No commandment in the Law of Moses prohibits visiting a Gentile; the restriction arose from purity concerns, especially about food, and was observed with varying strictness. “Unlawful” could suggest a scriptural rule that did not exist.

notes.phrase: Four days ago, at this very hour
notes.traditional: Four days ago I was fasting until this hour
notes.note: The Greek is awkward, literally “from the fourth day until this hour I was praying the ninth”. Most interpreters take it to mean that the vision came four days earlier at the same hour of the day, the ninth. Many later manuscripts add that Cornelius was fasting, which is the reading behind the KJV.

notes.phrase: You know the word that he sent
notes.note: The grammar of verses 36–38 is broken in Greek, and translators must supply connections. Here “the word” is taken as a first object of “you know” in verse 37, so the verb is repeated. Others link it back to verse 34 or treat it as a loose heading (“As for the word…”), and some manuscripts omit “that”, giving “He sent the word to the children of Israel”. The overall sense is not affected.

The Greek word means wood or anything made of it: a beam, a stake, or a tree. It refers here to the cross, and the phrase echoes Deuteronomy 21:22–23, where a body hung “on a tree” is under God’s curse. “Tree” is kept so that the scriptural allusion can be heard.

candidates.reason: The ritual sense (with the verb κοινόω) recurs in Mark 7, Acts 10–11, Romans 14 and Hebrews, and translations vary between common, profane, impure and defiled.
It recurs in Matthew 6, Luke and Acts, where “alms” is archaic and modern versions paraphrase inconsistently.
Used of the cross in Acts 5:30, 10:39, 13:29, Galatians 3:13 and 1 Peter 2:24 with an echo of Deuteronomy 21, and translators split between tree, wood, cross and gibbet.
For inspired speech in Acts 2, 10, 19 and 1 Corinthians 12–14 the choice between “tongues” and “languages” shapes how readers understand the phenomenon and should be uniform.
Numbered hours of the day recur across the Gospels and Acts, and a single policy is needed on keeping the ancient reckoning or converting to modern clock time.

warnings: Verse 45: πιστός is not rendered with a register form (faithful / believing) and has no register-exception note.
Verse 25: προσκυνέω is not rendered with a register form (worship; bow down before; pay homage; bow in worship) and has no register-exception note.
